answer: Within the supplied NLS extract (n=8,773; 236 BA-degree completions; 2.69% base rate), a Firth-corrected logistic regression of BA completion on socioeconomic status, race, and their interaction — with sex, ASVAB-ability composite, percentile-in-class and family-size as additive covariates, and White as the race-reference — finds **no statistically significant evidence that the SES-BA relationship differs across racial lines**. The joint test of the two SES×race interaction coefficients gives LR χ²(2) = 1.68 with p = 0.43 (unpenalised log-likelihood), with a Wald joint χ²(2) = 1.68 (p = 0.43) and a 1,000-rep bootstrap LR p = 0.66 all in agreement. Race-specific average marginal effects of SES on P(BA = 1) are similar in magnitude: White +0.72 pp per 1-SES-unit [bootstrap 95% CI −0.11, +1.50], Black +0.69 pp [+0.05, +1.29], Hispanic +0.30 pp [−0.48, +1.13]. Race-stratified Firth SES odds-ratios are 1.36 [1.05, 1.77] for White, 1.92 [1.09, 3.40] for Black, and 1.02 [0.50, 2.07] for Hispanic. The point estimates are consistent with a stronger SES effect among Black respondents, but the omnibus interaction test lacks statistical power (only 28 BA events for Black and 19 for Hispanic), so the data support neither a confident claim of moderation nor a confident claim of its absence — they surface a numerically suggestive but statistically unestablished pattern.

payload.hypothesis: Within the supplied NLS extract, race does not statistically moderate the SES-BA relationship once sex, ASVAB-ability, percentile-in-class and family-size are controlled and the Firth correction is applied (joint LR χ²(2) = 1.68, p = 0.43; Wald joint χ²(2) = 1.68, p = 0.43; 1,000-rep bootstrap LR p = 0.66). Race-specific SES average marginal effects on P(BA=1) are +0.72 pp per 1-SES-unit for White [bootstrap 95% CI −0.11, +1.50], +0.69 pp [+0.05, +1.29] for Black, and +0.30 pp [−0.48, +1.13] for Hispanic, broadly overlapping. Race-stratified SES odds ratios (1.36 / 1.92 / 1.02 for White / Black / Hispanic) point in a heterogeneous direction but the omnibus test does not reject the null of no moderation, and statistical power is constrained by only 28 and 19 BA completions in Black and Hispanic respondents respectively.
payload.workflow: Data ingested from /workspace/data/nls_ses_processed.csv (n=8773, no missing). Primary model: Firth-bias-corrected logistic regression (manual Newton-Raphson with bias-corrected score and unpenalised log-likelihood for inference) of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on SES, SAMPLE_RACE (White=reference), SES x SAMPLE_RACE, with additive SEX, ABILITY: COMPOSITE OF ASVAB SCORE, PERCENTILE IN CLASS, and FAMILY SIZE OF SAMPLE. Inference: (a) LR test on UNPENALISED Firth-fitted log-likelihoods (Heinze & Schemper 2002; Kosmidis & Firth 2017) because Firth penalty 0.5 log|I| differs across nested models and is therefore NOT chi-square distributed under H0; (b) Wald joint test of the two interaction coefficients; (c) nonparametric bootstrap (1,000 reps) of the LR statistics. Effect-size: race-specific Average Marginal Effect of SES on P(BA=1), in percentage-point units, with percentile bootstrap 95% CIs (n=1000). Supplementary: race-stratified Firth logistic regressions (same covariates, no interaction) reporting SES odds ratios and 95% CIs. Figure: predicted P(BA=1) vs SES, three lines (one per race), covariates at sample means, with bootstrap 95% shaded envelopes. Critical correction during execution: the naive Firth-PENALISED LR equals 43.2 because the penalty differs by ~20.8 between full and restricted models; that penalty difference contributes nearly the entire statistic, so it is reported as a diagnostic only and NOT used for inference.
